questions.question: What is community conservation, and why is it important?
questions.expected_answer: Local communities take part in managing and protecting natural resources and share the benefits (community-based natural resource management): rights and ownership, participation in decisions, shared benefits (jobs, tourism income, sustainable use), respect for local knowledge. Important because past exclusion caused resentment; when communities benefit they protect resources, report poaching and use resources sustainably; it reduces poverty and builds pride. Challenges: elite capture, lack of skills/money, crop damage, competing land needs.

questions.question: Describe two community conservation examples in South Africa.
questions.expected_answer: Makuleke: removed from Pafuri (northern Kruger) in 1969; land claim won in 1998 (about 24 000 ha); kept the land in the Kruger under contract with SANParks; partnered with private operators for lodges earning rent and jobs; young people trained as guides and rangers. Working for Water (1995): employs people from poor communities to clear invasive alien plants (wattles, pines, eucalyptus), creating jobs, increasing river flow and protecting biodiversity. Also food gardens, recycling, nurseries, small-scale fishing cooperatives.

questions.question: Explain eco-tourism, how it differs from mass tourism, and give an example.
questions.expected_answer: Eco-tourism is responsible travel to natural areas that conserves the environment, sustains local wellbeing and involves education: minimal impact (solar, water saving, recycling, local materials), supports conservation, benefits and respects local communities, educates. Mass tourism involves large numbers, big hotels and crowds, can damage the environment, and profits often leave the area. Examples: Makuleke lodges; Wild Coast/Amadiba community trails; Hermanus land-based whale watching (June-November); !Khwa ttu San Heritage Centre.
